title: Five Gummy Bears in NewJeans' Colors — The Evidence Behind ILLIT's Alleged 'Little Monsters' Diss
excerpt: Fans spotted five gummy bears in ILLIT's 'Little Monsters' music video matching NewJeans' signature member colors. With a court ruling acknowledging similarities and Google AI confusing the two groups, the controversy has reached a boiling point.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
"Five gummy bears. Five colors. Just a coincidence?"

On February 12, 2026, the Seoul Central District Court handed Min Hee-jin a landmark victory, ordering HYBE to pay approximately 25.5 billion KRW ($17.6 million) in the put option dispute. Buried in the ruling was a bombshell statement: **"Based on reports examining ILLIT's activities shortly after debut, there were aspects that could be judged as similar to NewJeans."**

And at that exact moment, K-pop fans unearthed a detail in ILLIT's 'Little Monsters' music video that sent the entire fandom into meltdown.

## The Five Gummy Bears — A Color-Coded Controversy

In ILLIT's 'Little Monsters' music video, there's a scene where the members eat gummy bears symbolizing the "monsters" within. What caught fans' attention wasn't the concept — it was the colors. **The five gummy bears appeared to match the five signature colors representing each NewJeans member.**

NewJeans' fandom, Bunnies, erupted immediately. "HYBE plans every single detail in their productions. You're telling us five gummy bears in five specific colors is random? Who believes that?" became the rallying cry.

ILLIT's defenders pushed back. They pointed out that the music video was conceptualized by external creative director Toshihiko Tanabe, making it illogical to assume BELIFT LAB or HYBE intentionally embedded a coded message targeting NewJeans. The gummy bears, they argued, simply represented the song's theme of confronting one's inner monsters.

But the controversy was far from over. What poured gasoline on the fire was the court ruling itself.

## The Court's Verdict — One Line That Changed Everything

In the put option ruling, a key issue was whether Min Hee-jin's dismissal was justified. HYBE argued she had destabilized the company by raising plagiarism allegations against ILLIT. Min Hee-jin's legal team countered that the plagiarism concerns were legitimate.

The court's response was devastating for HYBE: **"Insufficient evidence was found to deny that ILLIT bears similarities to NewJeans."** While the court stopped short of declaring outright plagiarism, it officially acknowledged that similarities exist as a matter of fact.

That single line in the ruling turned the K-pop world upside down. What had been dismissed as "fan opinion" or "fandom emotions" was now elevated to a **judicial finding** — a fundamentally different category of legitimacy.

![ILLIT-NewJeans similarity controversy — court ruling and fandom reactions](/images/news/illit-little-monsters-newjeans-five-colors-diss-1.webp)
_The court's acknowledgment of similarities reignited one of K-pop's most heated debates_

## When Google AI Joined the Fight

At the peak of the controversy, an experiment posted on Korean online community Instiz went mega-viral. When users fed photos of ILLIT members into Google's AI image recognition system, **the AI identified them as NewJeans members.**

The post exploded. "Even machines can't tell them apart" trended alongside "AI recognition depends on training data, so this proves nothing" — the debate split right down the middle.

From a technical standpoint, Google's image recognition analyzes not just facial features but styling, poses, color palettes, and overall aesthetic. If ILLIT and NewJeans share overlapping visual concepts, AI confusion is technically plausible. The question — whether this overlap represents **intentional copying** or **trend convergence** — is something AI fundamentally cannot answer.

But in the arena of fandom warfare, an experiment that looks like "scientific evidence" carries enormous weight, regardless of its methodological limitations.

## HYBE's Impossible Position

For HYBE and BELIFT LAB, this situation presents a classic no-win scenario.

Respond, and it reads as acknowledging the similarity. Stay silent, and it looks like there's nothing to refute. With a court having effectively validated the similarity claim, the space for asserting ILLIT's independent identity has shrunk dramatically.

Industry insiders note that ILLIT should have established a clearly differentiated musical and visual direction from their debut. The irony is that 'Magnetic' — their breakout debut hit — may have become a trap. Its early success reinforced the existing formula, making it harder to pivot away from the very comparisons that now haunt the group.

## MEARROW's Perspective on the ILLIT-NewJeans Saga

From MEARROW's analytical lens, this situation strikes at the heart of **IP strategy and risk management** in the K-pop industry.

"Concept similarity" has always been a gray area in K-pop. The line between following a trend and copying a specific artist is inherently blurry. But when a court acknowledges similarity and AI systems literally confuse two groups, it signals a **failure in establishing IP distinctiveness** at the agency level.

For trainees and aspiring idols, there's a critical lesson here. When choosing an agency, examine their artist IP strategy closely. Joining a company that replicates existing success models means potentially debuting into an endless cycle of "copycat" accusations. The ability to build your own unique identity matters more than the size of the company name.

## Looking Ahead

Five gummy bears. Five colors. Whether HYBE planted a deliberate message or it was pure coincidence may never be definitively answered.

But what's certain is this: a court acknowledged the similarities, AI couldn't distinguish the two groups, and fandom distrust has deepened further. The HYBE-Min Hee-jin war has entered a new chapter, and the battlefield has expanded from courtrooms to the color palette of gummy bears in a music video.

Whether ILLIT can escape this shadow and forge a truly independent identity — or remain permanently tagged as "NewJeans' shadow" — is the hottest question K-pop must answer in 2026.
